--- title: Introduction to R Programming --- # The Mission Throughout this unit we will use one running example to introduce the basic building blocks of R: vectors, strings, special values, matrices, data frames, lists, functions, file I/O, and graphics. **The mission:** a class of students has taken four quizzes. Each student's final grade is the average of their *best three* quiz scores -- that is, we drop each student's single lowest quiz score before averaging. To make things realistic, one student missed a quiz entirely, so we also need to handle a missing value correctly. We want to 1. work out the calculation step by step for one student, 2. package that calculation into a reusable function, 3. apply the function to every student to get a full set of results, and 4. present those results as a table and as plots. This mirrors how real data-analysis code is usually built: explore on one case, generalize into a function, then apply and report. # Step by Step, for One Student ## Vectors: recording quiz scores The score on each quiz, across all students, is naturally stored as a vector. Here are the scores for four quizzes and eight students (in the same order): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} quiz1 <- c(7,8,6,9,5,8,7,6) quiz2 <- c(8,7,5,9,6,7,8,5) quiz3 <- c(6,9,7,8,NA,9,6,7) quiz4 <- c(9,8,8,7,7,8,5,8) ``` ::: Notice the `NA` in `quiz3`: the fifth student missed that quiz. Ordinary arithmetic propagates a missing value rather than silently ignoring it, which is exactly the safe default we want: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} quiz3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 6 9 7 8 NA 9 6 7 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} mean(quiz3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] NA ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} mean(quiz3, na.rm = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 7.428571 ``` ::: ::: ## Strings: naming the quizzes and students We could type out `"Quiz1"`, `"Quiz2"`, ... by hand, but `paste0` builds such labels programmatically -- a habit that pays off the moment there are 40 quizzes instead of 4: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} quiz.names <- paste0("Quiz", 1:4) quiz.names ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Quiz1" "Quiz2" "Quiz3" "Quiz4" ``` ::: ::: The students' names are just another character vector: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} students <- c("Ava","Ben","Cleo","Dae","Ellis","Faye","Gus","Hana") students ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Ava" "Ben" "Cleo" "Dae" "Ellis" "Faye" "Gus" "Hana" ``` ::: ::: `sprintf` is useful for turning numbers back into readable text, for example a one-line summary for a single student: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sprintf("%s's scores were: %s", students[5], paste(c(quiz1[5],quiz2[5],quiz3[5],quiz4[5]), collapse = ", ")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Ellis's scores were: 5, 6, NA, 7" ``` ::: ::: ## Matrices: all students, all quizzes, at once Binding the four quiz vectors together as columns gives a matrix with one row per student and one column per quiz. We then attach the row and column names we just built: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} scores <- cbind(quiz1,quiz2,quiz3,quiz4) colnames(scores) <- quiz.names rownames(scores) <- students scores ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Quiz1 Quiz2 Quiz3 Quiz4 Ava 7 8 6 9 Ben 8 7 9 8 Cleo 6 5 7 8 Dae 9 9 8 7 Ellis 5 6 NA 7 Faye 8 7 9 8 Gus 7 8 6 5 Hana 6 5 7 8 ``` ::: ::: A matrix is indexed as `[row, column]`. This lets us pull out one student's record, one quiz's results, or a logical selection such as "every score above 8": ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} scores["Ellis", ] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Quiz1 Quiz2 Quiz3 Quiz4 5 6 NA 7 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} scores[, "Quiz1"] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Ava Ben Cleo Dae Ellis Faye Gus Hana 7 8 6 9 5 8 7 6 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} scores[scores > 8] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 9 9 9 NA 9 9 ``` ::: ::: ## Special values: a missing quiz `is.na` locates missing values anywhere in an object, including a whole matrix at once, and `which(..., arr.ind = TRUE)` reports their row/column position: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} is.na(scores) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Quiz1 Quiz2 Quiz3 Quiz4 Ava FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE Ben FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE Cleo FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE Dae FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE Ellis FALSE FALSE TRUE FALSE Faye FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE Gus FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE Hana FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} which(is.na(scores), arr.ind = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` row col Ellis 5 3 ``` ::: ::: It is worth knowing what happens in the extreme case where a student has *no* recorded quiz at all: taking the mean of zero numbers is not zero, it is undefined, and R represents that with `NaN` ("not a number") rather than `NA`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mean(numeric(0)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] NaN ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} is.nan(mean(numeric(0))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: We will rely on this distinction later, so that our function can automatically flag a student with no data at all. ## Data frames: adding names and gender A data frame lets us combine columns of different types -- here, the students' names and gender alongside their (numeric) quiz scores -- into a single table: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gender <- factor(c("f","m","f","m","f","f","m","f")) roster <- data.frame(name = students, gender = gender, scores) roster ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: Because the row names of `scores` were dropped when it became columns of `roster`, we now identify students by the `name` column instead. `grep` can find, by pattern, which columns hold quiz scores -- handy since we built those names programmatically earlier: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} quiz.cols <- grep("^Quiz", names(roster)) quiz.cols ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3 4 5 6 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} names(roster)[quiz.cols] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Quiz1" "Quiz2" "Quiz3" "Quiz4" ``` ::: ::: The usual data-frame subsetting tools -- `[ , ]`, `$`, and `subset` -- work as expected, and `tapply` lets us summarize a column by group, e.g. the average `Quiz1` score by gender: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} roster[roster$gender == "f", ] ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} subset(roster, Quiz1 > 7) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} tapply(roster$Quiz1, roster$gender, mean) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` f m 6.4 8.0 ``` ::: ::: ## Lists: packaging one student's full result We now have everything needed to work out Ellis's final grade by hand. A **list** is the natural container for the result, because it bundles pieces of different shapes -- the raw scores, the scores kept, the score dropped, and a single final number -- under one name: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ellis <- as.numeric(roster[roster$name == "Ellis", quiz.cols]) ellis ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 5 6 NA 7 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} valid <- ellis[!is.na(ellis)] valid ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 5 6 7 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} i.min <- which.min(valid) kept <- valid[-i.min] final <- mean(kept) result <- list(raw = ellis, kept = kept, dropped = valid[i.min], final = final) result ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $raw [1] 5 6 NA 7 $kept [1] 6 7 $dropped [1] 5 $final [1] 6.5 ``` ::: ::: This confirms the calculation for one student. The rest of the unit turns this scratch work into something we can reuse and apply to everyone. # Writing the Core Function ## A loop-based implementation Before relying on `which.min`, it is worth seeing explicitly how a computer finds a minimum: by walking through the values one at a time and remembering the smallest one seen so far. This is the same control-flow pattern (a `for` loop with an `if` inside) used throughout numerical computing: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} find.lowest <- function(x) { n <- length(x) i.min <- 1 x.min <- x[1] if(n > 1) { for(i in 2:n) { if(x[i] < x.min) { x.min <- x[i] i.min <- i } } } list(value = x.min, index = i.min) } find.lowest(valid) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $value [1] 5 $index [1] 1 ``` ::: ::: ## A vectorized implementation R's built-in `which.min` (and, for dropping more than one value, `order`) does the same job in one call, and is what we will use going forward: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} which.min(valid) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} order(valid) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 2 3 ``` ::: ::: We now wrap the full calculation -- discard missing quizzes, drop the lowest remaining score(s), average what's left -- into one function. Passing `n.drop` as an argument (rather than hard-coding "drop 1") makes the function reusable for a different grading policy later. Following the special-value discussion above, a student with no valid quiz at all correctly returns `NaN` instead of causing an error: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} compute.final.grade <- function(scores, n.drop = 1) { valid <- scores[!is.na(scores)] if(length(valid) == 0) { return(list(raw = scores, kept = numeric(0), dropped = numeric(0), final = NaN)) } #never drop every remaining score n.drop <- min(n.drop, length(valid) - 1) if(n.drop > 0) { drop.ix <- order(valid)[1:n.drop] dropped <- valid[drop.ix] kept <- valid[-drop.ix] } else { dropped <- numeric(0) kept <- valid } list(raw = scores, kept = kept, dropped = dropped, final = mean(kept)) } ``` ::: Checking the function against the by-hand result for Ellis, and against the all-missing edge case: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} compute.final.grade(ellis) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $raw [1] 5 6 NA 7 $kept [1] 6 7 $dropped [1] 5 $final [1] 6.5 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} compute.final.grade(c(NA,NA,NA,NA)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $raw [1] NA NA NA NA $kept numeric(0) $dropped numeric(0) $final [1] NaN ``` ::: ::: # Applying the Function to Every Student `apply(X, 1, FUN)` calls `FUN` once per **row** of `X` -- exactly what we need to run `compute.final.grade` on every student's four quiz scores: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} final.scores <- apply(roster[, quiz.cols], 1, function(x) compute.final.grade(x)$final) final.scores ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Ava Ben Cleo Dae Ellis Faye Gus Hana 8.000000 8.333333 7.000000 8.666667 6.500000 8.333333 7.000000 7.000000 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} roster$final <- final.scores ``` ::: The dropped score for each student is extracted the same way, and both new columns are added to `roster`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} roster$dropped <- sapply(1:nrow(roster), function(i) { r <- compute.final.grade(as.numeric(roster[i, quiz.cols])) if(length(r$dropped) == 0) NA else r$dropped }) roster ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: It is instructive to compare this with a *fully vectorized* alternative that needs no per-student function call at all: if we did **not** need to drop a quiz, the weighted total for every student could be computed in one line via matrix multiplication of the score matrix by a vector of weights: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} w <- rep(1/4, 4) as.matrix(roster[, quiz.cols]) %*% w ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] Ava 7.50 Ben 8.00 Cleo 6.50 Dae 8.25 Ellis NA Faye 8.00 Gus 6.50 Hana 6.50 ``` ::: ::: Notice that Ellis's entry comes back as `NA` -- matrix multiplication has no way to skip a missing value on its own. This is precisely why we wrote `compute.final.grade`: it encodes the extra logic (ignore missing quizzes, then drop the lowest) that a single matrix operation cannot express. ## Saving and reloading the results The final `roster` is worth keeping. A data frame can be written as a plain csv file for spreadsheets, or saved as an `.RDS` file to preserve it exactly (including the `gender` factor) for future R sessions: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} write.csv(roster, file = "roster.csv", row.names = FALSE) saveRDS(roster, file = "roster.RDS") roster.reloaded <- readRDS("roster.RDS") identical(roster, roster.reloaded) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: # Presenting the Results ## Base R graphics A quick histogram shows the distribution of final grades, with a vertical line marking the class average: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hist(roster$final, breaks = 5, col = "lightblue", main = "Distribution of Final Grades", xlab = "Final Grade") abline(v = mean(roster$final), col = "red", lwd = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](unit01_introduction_longer_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: A side-by-side boxplot compares the two gender groups: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} boxplot(final ~ gender, data = roster, main = "Final Grade by Gender", xlab = "Gender", ylab = "Final Grade") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](unit01_introduction_longer_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-23-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## ggplot2 **ggplot2** builds the same kind of comparison declaratively, by mapping columns of `roster` to visual properties and layering geometries with `+`. Here the boxplot is enhanced with the individual student scores jittered on top: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ggplot2) ggplot(roster, aes(x = gender, y = final, fill = gender)) + geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE, alpha = 0.6) + geom_jitter(width = 0.1, size = 2) + labs( title = "Final Grade by Gender", x = "Gender", y = "Final Grade" ) + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](unit01_introduction_longer_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: We can also ask a natural follow-up question -- does a strong first quiz predict a strong final grade? -- with a scatter plot colored by gender: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(roster, aes(x = Quiz1, y = final, color = gender)) + geom_point(size = 2) + labs( title = "Final Grade vs. Quiz 1 Score", x = "Quiz 1 Score", y = "Final Grade", color = "Gender" ) + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](unit01_introduction_longer_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-25-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## gt Finally, **gt** turns `roster` into a polished report table instead of a plain printout: a title, grouped "Quizzes" columns, one decimal place on the computed grade, and a readable symbol for Ellis's missing quiz. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(gt) roster |> gt(rowname_col = "name") |> tab_header( title = "Course Grade Report", subtitle = "Each student's lowest quiz score is dropped" ) |> sub_missing(columns = everything(), missing_text = "—") |> fmt_number(columns = final, decimals = 1) |> cols_label( gender = "Gender", dropped = "Dropped Score", final = "Final Grade" ) |> tab_spanner(label = "Quizzes", columns = c(Quiz1, Quiz2, Quiz3, Quiz4)) |> tab_stubhead(label = "Student") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
